data.gender_notes: Asifah is used as a unisex name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: From the Arabic word ‘Asafa’ which means ‘to help’ or ‘to support’. In Islamic tradition, Asifah is a name for a helper or supporter. The name is mentioned in various Hadiths, where the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) is reported to have given it as a name to his companions. The name Asifah carries the meaning “Helpful, Supportive” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Asifah usually hope their child will grow to embody helpful, supportive and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.spiritual_meaning: Symbol of support and help in times of need.
data.etymology: Asifah belongs to the Arabic linguistic tradition and is used in Islamic naming. Its recorded meaning is “Helpful, Supportive.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Asifah total 8, giving a life-path number of 8. Number 8 is linked with Saturn and with the qualities of ambition, resilience and material success.

historical_references.reference: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh al-Buldan. The Conquests of the Levant: Muhammad ibn Ruzzik's Chronicle of the Crusades. Translated by P.K. Hitti. New York: Columbia University Press, 1922.
historical_references.context: Asifah bint Artuq, the daughter of the Artuqid ruler of Mardin, played a significant role in the Islamic defense against the Crusaders. She was married to the Ayyubid ruler of Aleppo, Tughtegin, and after his death, she married Zengi, the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty, in around 1128. Asifah's strategic marriages helped strengthen the Islamic forces against the Crusaders.

historical_references.reference: Ibn al-Athir, Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh. The Complete History: A World History from the Founding of Islam to the Present. Translated by J.S. Richards. New York: Garnet Publishing, 1993.
historical_references.context: Asifah bint Bahadur, the wife of Malik al-Salih Ayyub of Egypt, played a crucial role in the defense of Egypt against the Mongols. In 1260, during the Battle of Ain Jalut, she disguised herself as a man and fought alongside the army, which helped to confuse and disorient the Mongols, contributing to the Islamic victory.
